headline: Middesk Inc clears identity and operating comfortably for SMB account opening. The decision rests on open liens and litigation, which this record establishes exist but cannot size.

confirmed.text: Identity is settled on every axis the registries can speak to. The submitted name and address both match state registrations, entity type is confirmed against the Delaware filing, and the company holds an active registration in at least one state including the state of its submitted address. Formed in 2018, it is not a recently stood-up entity, and a submitted person matches an officer on a state registration — the strongest control-person evidence registry data produces.

It is visibly operating rather than merely registered. The address is commercial and deliverable, the website is reachable, and the domain registrant corroborates the business at high confidence, with the site's own name and address matching what was submitted. For account opening that combination does most of the work: registry data proves an entity exists, and this is what shows someone is running it.

Screening is clean where it matters most. Watchlist and PEP returned no hits, no prohibited industry was identified, and there are no bankruptcy filings. Adverse media returned hits the provider itself scored low, which is worth an analyst's glance rather than an escalation.

Open liens were found and litigation records were returned. This is the only thing on the record that points at the business rather than at the limits of the data, and it is what the decision should turn on.

Two things look irregular and are not. Registration status is mixed — active in some states, inactive in others — which is ordinary housekeeping for a company registered across many states rather than a sign of lapse. And five addresses on the record are each shared with more than a hundred businesses, which is the expected shape of registered-agent addresses, not a shell pattern.

couldNotConfirm.point: Standing in Delaware, and the status of several registrations that returned nothing at all
couldNotConfirm.wouldAnswer: Delaware publishes no good-standing sub-status for any company, so no order will produce it — a Certificate of Good Standing from the customer is the only route. Separately, the formation-state status and several others came back unresolved rather than negative, which a re-run of the registration search may clear.

couldNotConfirm.point: What the liens and litigation actually are
couldNotConfirm.wouldAnswer: The record establishes that they exist and stops there — no amounts, no dates, no indication of whether they are satisfied. Ordering the lien and litigation detail is the single thing standing between this file and a decision.

couldNotConfirm.point: Whether the person named on the website is the person submitted
couldNotConfirm.wouldAnswer: The website person check came back unverified — the site does not name them in a form the check could match. The officer match on the state registration already covers this ground more authoritatively.

couldNotConfirm.point: Who ultimately owns or benefits from the business
couldNotConfirm.wouldAnswer: No beneficial-ownership insight exists in the catalog; ownership is only ever implied from the people filings happen to name. If your policy requires a UBO determination it cannot be satisfied from this record by any order.

actions: Treat identity as answered and route this file on the liens and litigation alone. Name, address, entity type, an officer and an independent website all corroborate — re-confirming identity would be spending review time in the wrong place.
If standing is a gating requirement, ask the customer for the certificate rather than waiting on an order that will never return one.
data: Order the lien and litigation detail — amounts, dates, and whether satisfied. Everything else is decided.
Re-run the registration search to resolve the filings that returned no status, if the mixed picture matters to your risk tier.
